explanations.explanation: Old habits are hard to break, baker, but Balaam breaks this one. Verse 1 says “…he did not seek omens as on previous occasions…” It happens because he saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel. I know a thing or two about skipping my usual routine, like the day I walked past a full cooling rack of cookies. Okay, that never happened.

Right, he skips the omens this time. The text says he “…did not seek omens as on previous occasions…” (Numbers 24:1). He saw that it pleased the LORD to bless Israel, and that settled it. Three hilltops in, Balaam finally stops running the old routine.

Yes, he turns his face toward the wilderness. That's the direction he looks instead of going off for omens. From there he lifts his eyes and sees Israel camped tribe by tribe. Nice and simple, friend. Sometimes the answer is just where the text points.

The sea is a fair guess, baker, but verse 1 never mentions it. The text says Balaam “…turned his face toward the wilderness.” It's a dry, wide-open view, and that's where Israel's camp was spread out. Think sand, not waves.

Mountains feel right because Balaam is up on a high place, I'll give you that. But verse 1 says he turned his face toward the wilderness, not the mountains. Where he stands and where he looks are two different things. Even I mix those up when I'm standing on my gold base looking at the oven.

That's it, the Spirit of God comes upon him. Verse 2 says it happens as he looks up and sees Israel encamped tribe by tribe. Then he lifts up an oracle, a spoken message. Balak wanted a curse, and the Spirit of God had other plans for that mouth.

I can see why fear came to mind, with an angry king standing right there. But the text doesn't mention fear at all. Verse 2 says “…the Spirit of God came upon him…” After that, Balaam starts speaking. Whatever Balak was feeling, that's not what came upon Balaam.

Glory is a big, beautiful word, baker, and it's close. But verse 2 uses a different one: “…the Spirit of God came upon him…” The words of the oracle that follow come right after that. It's a small word swap that changes the whole sentence, like grabbing butterscotch bits when the recipe says raisins.

explanations.answer: Gardens and trees growing by water
explanations.explanation: You've got it. Verse 6 says Israel's camp is spread out “like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters.” That's a whole lot of green and a whole lot of water. Balaam came to curse them and ended up writing a landscaping brochure.

explanations.answer: Walls and towers built for battle
explanations.explanation: A camp full of tribes could sound like a fortress, I get that. But verse 6 never mentions a wall or a tower. Balaam says the camp is like palm groves, gardens beside a stream and cedars beside the waters. It's a picture of growing things, not defending things.

explanations.answer: Flocks and herds resting in green fields
explanations.explanation: Green fields is a nice picture, and you're in the right neighborhood. But verse 6 doesn't mention flocks or herds. It says “like palm groves, like gardens beside a stream, like aloes the LORD has planted, like cedars beside the waters.” Everything he names is something planted and growing near water.

True, and verse 7 says it plainly: “His king will be greater than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted.” Agag is a name the Bible later gives to a king of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:8). So Balaam is saying Israel's king will be greater than a king. That's a lot of good news from a man who was hired to deliver bad news.

Not quite, baker. Verse 7 says “His king will be greater than Agag, and his kingdom will be exalted.” Agag is a name the Bible later gives to a king of the Amalekites (1 Samuel 15:8). So the king of Israel comes out greater, not lesser. Balaam isn't shrinking anybody here.

Yes, that's the line. Verse 9 ends, “Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you.” Now think about who invited Balaam out here to curse Israel. Balak, king of Moab, is standing right there hearing it.

explanations.answer: They are spared in the end
explanations.explanation: That would be a soft landing, but it isn't what Balaam says. Verse 9 ends, “Blessed are those who bless you and cursed are those who curse you.” Nobody gets spared for cursing in that line. Balaam says it straight.

Close to the right neighborhood, baker, but those aren't the words. Verse 9 says, “…cursed are those who curse you.” The text doesn't say anything about being forgotten. The word is cursed, and it comes right after the word blessed.

Three, that's the count. Balak says, “I summoned you to curse my enemies, but behold, you have persisted in blessing them these three times.” He's been keeping score, and he is not happy with the total. When someone keeps count out loud like that, you know the patience is gone.

Two is close, and I bet you were counting the earlier oracles. But Balak says “…you have persisted in blessing them these three times.” This oracle in chapter 24 is the third one. Balak is counting every blessing he didn't ask for.
Seven sounds important, I know. But Balak's complaint in verse 10 is “…you have persisted in blessing them these three times.” Seven isn't in that sentence at all. Three blessings was plenty for him.

explanations.answer: Flee at once to your home
explanations.explanation: That's it. Balak says, “Therefore, flee at once to your home!” He adds that he said he would reward Balaam richly, but the LORD has denied the reward. He's done with the hilltops, the oracles and Balaam. That's what a king sounds like when he's out of patience.

explanations.answer: Try again from a fourth hilltop
explanations.explanation: A fourth try would be one more round of the same, and Balak is finished with that. In verse 11 he says, “Therefore, flee at once to your home!” He's sending Balaam away, not moving him to a new spot. Three blessings were enough for him.

Altars aren't on Balak's mind anymore. Verse 11 says, “Therefore, flee at once to your home!” He even says the LORD has denied Balaam's reward. Balak is sending him home, not setting up another round.

True, and it's Balak himself who says it. Verse 11 reads, “I said I would reward you richly, but instead the LORD has denied your reward.” Even the angry king names the LORD as the reason the pay isn't coming. I think that's quite an admission to make while yelling.

The text says otherwise, baker. In verse 11 Balak tells Balaam, “I said I would reward you richly, but instead the LORD has denied your reward.” So it's the LORD he names. Balak says it himself, right in the middle of being upset.

explanations.answer: Go beyond the command of the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's what Balaam says, and he says it firmly. In verse 13 he says no amount of silver and gold from Balak's house could get him to do anything “…to go beyond the command of the LORD.” Then he adds, “I must speak whatever the LORD says.” A whole house full of silver and gold, and the answer is still no.

explanations.answer: Leave his own people behind for good
explanations.explanation: That's not what he says, friend. In verse 14 he tells Balak, “Now I am going back to my people…” So he's headed home. What silver and gold couldn't buy was going “…beyond the command of the LORD.” (Numbers 24:13)

explanations.answer: Bless the people of Moab instead
explanations.explanation: Blessing Moab never comes up in verse 13. What Balaam says is that he could not do anything of his own accord “…to go beyond the command of the LORD.” That's the one thing a house full of silver and gold can't get from him. The topic is the command of the LORD, not who gets blessed.

explanations.answer: A warning about what Israel will do to Moab
explanations.explanation: That's the offer. Balaam says, “…let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come.” Balak is the king of Moab, so those are Balak's people. Balaam is leaving, but he's not leaving quietly.

explanations.answer: A promise to come back and try once more
explanations.explanation: Balaam isn't promising a comeback, baker. He says, “Now I am going back to my people…” Then he offers something else: a warning about what this people will do to Balak's people in the days to come. This is his goodbye, not a see you later.

explanations.answer: A blessing on Moab for the days ahead
explanations.explanation: A blessing on Moab would have made Balak's day, but verse 14 says otherwise. Balaam says, “…let me warn you what this people will do to your people in the days to come.” Warn is the key word there. It's a heads-up, not a blessing.
That's the idea. Balaam says, “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near.” Not now and not near both point to a time down the road. He's looking ahead, and it isn't today.

That would be looking backward, and Balaam is looking ahead. Verse 17 says, “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near.” Not now means it hasn't happened yet. Whoever he sees is still on the way.

explanations.answer: He's in Israel's camp right now
explanations.explanation: Balaam is standing right over the camp, so I see why you'd think that. But verse 17 says, “I see him, but not now; I behold him, but not near.” Not now and not near means he isn't down there today. The one he sees is coming later on.

explanations.answer: A king rising up from Israel
explanations.explanation: Yes, a king. Verse 17 says, “A star will come forth from Jacob, and a scepter will arise from Israel.” Then verse 19 adds, “A ruler will come from Jacob…” Star, scepter and ruler all point the same way.

explanations.answer: A temple rising up in Israel
explanations.explanation: A temple is a big, impressive picture, but that's not what he describes. A star comes forth, a scepter arises, and then verse 19 says, “A ruler will come from Jacob…” Those are all about a person, not a building. Someone is coming.

explanations.answer: A harvest rising up in Israel
explanations.explanation: Harvest has a nice ring to it, especially after the garden pictures earlier. But in verse 17, Balaam says a star will come forth and a scepter will arise. Verse 19 follows with “A ruler will come from Jacob…” So he's talking about a ruler, not a crop.

Moab it is. Verse 17 says, “He will crush the skulls of Moab…” Balak is king of Moab, so Balaam is delivering this news right to his face. Hard moment for him to hear, and he asked for this guy to come.

Egypt does show up in this passage, baker, but not here. In verse 8 Balaam says God brought Israel out of Egypt. In verse 17 the one who will crush skulls does it to Moab. The two names come from two different lines.

Aram never shows up in this passage, so that one's a stray. Verse 17 says, “He will crush the skulls of Moab and strike down all the sons of Sheth.” Balaam is talking to Balak, king of Moab, and that's the nation he names. It's the one standing in front of him.
True. Verse 18 says, “Edom will become a possession, as will Seir, his enemy…” Edom is the nation that came from Esau (Genesis 36:9). Balaam is just going down the list, one nation after another.

Not quite, friend. Verse 18 says, “Edom will become a possession, as will Seir, his enemy…” Edom is the nation that came from Esau (Genesis 36:9). So the word is possession, and it's right there in the text.

That's the word. Verse 20 says, “Amalek was first among the nations, but his end is destruction.” Amalek is the nation that attacked Israel at Rephidim (Exodus 17:8). First place at the start, and that line ends in destruction.

Peace would be a happier ending, baker, but that's not what Balaam says. Verse 20 reads, “Amalek was first among the nations, but his end is destruction.” The word “but” in that line is a big turn. First at the start, destruction at the end.

I see why that came to mind, since the verse does say Amalek was first among the nations. But it keeps going: “…but his end is destruction.” Greatness is how it starts, and destruction is how it ends. That “but” in the middle does a lot of work.

I get it, the cliff nest sounds like the safest address around. Verse 21 does say, “Your dwelling place is secure, and your nest is set in a cliff.” But the very next line turns: “Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.” So the text never promises safe forever. The cliff nest doesn't get the last word.

Right, the text doesn't promise that. Verse 21 says, “Your dwelling place is secure, and your nest is set in a cliff.” Then verse 22 says, “Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.” That little word “yet” is where the good news stops.
That's the name. Verse 22 says, “Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.” It's a short name in a short line, but the line is heavy. A secure place on a cliff, and then a captor.

Egypt is a name you'll meet a lot in the Bible, but it's not the one here. In this passage Egypt shows up in verse 8, where God brought Israel out of it. The captor in verse 22 is named Asshur. Different line, different name.

Babylon is a famous name, so I understand the guess. But it doesn't appear anywhere in this passage. Verse 22 says, “Yet Kain will be destroyed when Asshur takes you captive.” Asshur is the name Balaam gives.

Perish is the word. Verse 24 says, “Ships will come from the coasts of Cyprus; they will subdue Asshur and Eber, but they too will perish forever.” Notice the “too” in there. Even the ones who come out on top in this line don't stay on top.

Ruling sounds like the natural next step after subduing somebody. But verse 24 says the ships “…will subdue Asshur and Eber, but they too will perish forever.” That “but” turns the sentence around. Subduing comes first, and perishing comes last.

Remain would be a nice, steady ending, baker, but it's not what Balaam says. Verse 24 ends, “…they too will perish forever.” The ships win for a moment, then the line closes on the opposite word. It's like a fresh cookie that never makes it to the box.

True, and it's a quiet ending. Verse 25 says, “Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.” After all that shouting and clapping, they just walk off in different directions. The oracles stay in the record, though.

The text says otherwise. Verse 25 reads, “Then Balaam arose and returned to his homeland, and Balak also went on his way.” So Balaam heads home and Balak goes his own way. Neither one is left standing on that hilltop.
